newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian U.N. lawyer files defence in libel case.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian U.N. lawyer files defence in libel case.

text.p: The U.N Special Rapporteur on Judges and the Judiciary said on Saturday he has reluctantly filed a defence in a $24 million libel suit, although the United Nations maintains he has immunity from such suits. The special rapporteur, Malaysian lawyer Param Cumaraswamy, said he was forced to file the defence on Friday after the Malaysian Court of Appeals refused his request for a stay. "I was forced to file this defence, which I have done under very severe protest," Param said in a telephone interview.
U.N. human rights investigators on Friday closed ranks around Param, urging U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan in a joint letter to take further steps to protect his immunity.

Earlier this week, Param was hit with a second 60 million ringgit ($24 million) suit. The suit was filed by a Malaysian lawyer who said he was defamed by remarks Param made in an article published in the November 1995 issue of the International Commercial Litigation magazine, a London-based publication.

In the article, Param was quoted as saying he was investigating complaints that businessmen were manipulating the Malaysian judicial system. MBf Capital and MBf Northern Securities filed the first suit and Malaysian lawyer V. Kanagalingam filed the second over Param's comments in the article.
Param said the core of his defence is that the observations he made in the journal article are true and have also been made by top Malaysian leaders.

"Very simply I have pleaded the truth of the comments I made," he said. "The same concerns were expressed subsequently and in a similar vein by the Prime Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister, even the Chief Justice, and earlier by the judge who heard these matters in court."
Param said he was touched by the support from his U.N. colleagues.

In the joint letter, the 30 experts argued that immunity from legal process granted to U.N. specialists under a 1946 convention had been undermined by the Malaysian courts and asked Annan to take further steps to protect Param.
"They will have no difficulty getting that from the secretary-general, who feels strong about this matter," said U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard in New York. "It is a matter of principle."
Eckhard did not say what Annan would do. However, U.N. sources said officials were consulting with Malaysia, including Razali Ismail, its U.N. envoy and this year's General Assembly president.
U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Ralph Zacklin said the world body regarded the matter with the "utmost seriousness and urgency".

Annan waded into the lawsuit last March, submitting a certificate to the court asserting Param enjoyed the protections provided under the Convention on Privileges and Immunities of the United Nations.

"Threatening the immunity of one expert constitutes an attack on the entire system and institution of the United Nations special (human rights) procedures and mechanisms," the human rights envoys said in their letter.
It stopped short of calls by some non-governmental organisations urging Annan to take the case of Param's immunity immediately to the International Court of Justice.

On June 28, Malaysian Judicial Commissioner Zainun Ali dismissed with costs Param's application to strike out the suit. She ordered him to file his defence, but said he could cite evidence at the trial to support his claim of immunity.
